source.title: What causes the test error? Going beyond bias-variance via ANOVA

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present; no apparent cutoff or garbling affecting the study.
record.tranche_reason: The study derives and evaluates risk curves for two-layer random-feature networks and linear regression, using theoretical analysis and simulations rather than reproducing the original deep-network experiments.
record.gate_note: The paper's discussions of double descent and results attributed to other studies are not recorded as rows. Theoretical heatmaps and empirical plots often provide no exact risk values; qualitative outcomes are recorded as stated. The paper does not vary training epochs.
record.test_reason: The paper derives asymptotic test MSE for orthogonally initialized two-layer random-feature networks (linear and nonlinear) and for ridge linear regression. It shows a risk peak at the interpolation threshold p/n = 1 under a small fixed ridge penalty, in both the sample and parametrization directions. It shows the peak is variance-driven and vanishes under optimal ridge. It checks the sample-wise behaviour on one real dataset. These are its own results on V3, V4 and V6, from a different method than the originals. These are random-feature models with only the second layer trained and p ≤ d, not deep networks, so V1 is not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors' main aim is an ANOVA decomposition of the variance. They find the sample–initialization interaction often dominates the variance and diverges at the interpolation threshold as λ → 0. A small fixed ridge produces double-descent or unimodal MSE through this variance. Optimally tuned ridge (or ensembling) removes the MSE peak, while the variance itself is often unimodal. They also characterize phase transitions between monotone and unimodal variance.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses asymptotic random-matrix analysis, simulation, and an empirical regression dataset for orthogonally initialized two-layer random-feature networks and linear regression; it does not reproduce the original deep-network experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported risk shape depends on the ridge penalty (fixed small versus optimally tuned), parametrization π, data aspect ratio δ, and, in the empirical study, dataset and sample size.

fits_no_version.finding: The ANOVA decomposition shows the sample–initialization interaction Vsi dominates the variance at the interpolation threshold. It exceeds the main effects, and ensembling can remove it.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The double-descent peak in random-feature models comes mainly from the interaction between training-sample and initialization randomness, not from either source alone.

record.problems: The main theory relies on proportional asymptotics and specific random-feature or linear models. The empirical study uses one dataset and reports plotted means and standard deviations without exact curve values in the text. Several theoretical curve results are described qualitatively. No epochs are studied.
record.rows_left_out: No results beyond the 60-row limit. R12 is an accidental duplicate placeholder for the π = 0.2 selected-penalty result already recorded in R10 and should not be counted as a separate result; remove R12. The general-covariance simulations in Section 4.3 are not separately extracted because the text gives qualitative observations about non-monotonicity and variance components without a distinct curve result needed beyond the rows above.

untested.parts: All of it. No deep networks are studied, only two-layer random-feature models with p ≤ d.
All of it. There is no training-time or epoch axis.
Model classes beyond random features and ridge regression. Large overparametrization is not reached, because π ≤ 1 caps p at d.
All of it. No single complexity measure is tested as a predictor of peak location across size, epochs and samples.
Label noise is fixed at σ = 0.3, so noise is not varied to show it drives the peak. Multiple or triple descent is not tested.

missing.what: Under optimal λ* the variance can stay unimodal (non-monotone) even though the MSE peak vanishes. Optimal ridge removes the MSE peak but not the variance non-monotonicity.
AR-1 general-covariance simulations (r = 0.5, 0.9; λ = 0.01 and 0.001) still show non-monotone MSE and variance at the threshold. The dominant terms shift to Vsl and Vsli at r = 0.9.
With fixed λ and δ < 1, the MSE decreases monotonically in π with no double descent. Here γ < 1, so the threshold is never reached.
The authors state they found no evidence of multiple descent in the proportional regime.

record.verdict_notes: V1 is dropped because the systems are two-layer random-feature models, not deep networks. π ≤ 1 (p ≤ d) limits how far past the threshold the models go. Proposition 6 (R6) varies dimension together with capacity, so it is not a clean capacity sweep. The paper cites Nakkiran et al. (an original source) but is not itself an original source.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test the original deep-network settings; its main network results concern two-layer networks trained only in the second layer. The empirical sample-size and parameterization sweeps use one dataset.
No test-error sweep over training epochs or training time.
Does not establish that more data hurts generally; data-hurt behavior is assessed for particular regularization choices, model conditions, and one empirical dataset.
Tests selected two-layer network and linear-regression models, not model classes generally.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested as a predictor of peak locations across size, epochs, and sample size.
Studies variance and regularization effects, but does not test whether label noise drives the peak across settings or whether optimally tuned regularization eliminates multiple or triple descent.
Does not compare the curve with an alternative effective parameter count to determine whether a second descent is an artifact.

rows.subject: two-layer linear neural network (orthogonal initialization; ridge regression)
rows.operation_detail: Theoretical asymptotic MSE as the sample size changes, plotted against 1/δ = n/d.
rows.value: The MSE is described as unimodal when π is small, with π = 0.5 as an example; the paper says there may be no double descent when δ is sufficiently small.

rows.check: The state was wrong. MSE that is unimodal in n means error first rises with more samples, which is the V3 effect. It lacks only the initial descent of double descent. V6 removed.

rows.subject: two-layer linear neural network (orthogonal initialization; ridge regression)
rows.size_stated: p intermediate features; parametrization level π = p/d
rows.operation_detail: Theoretical asymptotic MSE over parametrization with the ridge penalty set to its optimum.
rows.value: The MSE is non-increasing as a function of π, holding δ fixed.
rows.note: This is an explicit monotonicity result under optimally tuned ridge regularization.
rows.check: The state was wrong: under optimal λ* the MSE is non-increasing in π, so the peak disappears, as V6 says. V1 and V4 removed: this is a regularization condition, not a capacity curve contradicting V4.

rows.subject: two-layer linear neural network (orthogonal initialization; ridge regression)
rows.size_stated: p intermediate features; parametrization level π = p/d
rows.operation_detail: Theoretical asymptotic MSE over data aspect ratio with the ridge penalty set to its optimum.
rows.value: The MSE is increasing as a function of δ = d/n, holding π fixed.
rows.note: Since increasing sample size decreases δ, this result describes decreasing MSE as sample size increases in the tested asymptotic setting.
rows.check: Under optimal λ* the MSE rises with δ, so it falls as n grows: the more-data-hurts effect is absent rather than reversed. For V6 this row is observed, since the peak vanishes under optimal ridge.

source_check.correct: State by version: V3 absent; V6 observed. At optimal λ*, MSE is non-decreasing in δ and therefore non-increasing in n at fixed d and π.
source_check.problem: The shared absent state fits V3 but contradicts V6, whose predicted removal of the MSE peak is observed.

rows.subject: ordinary linear regression with optimally tuned ridge regression
rows.operation_detail: Theoretical limiting MSE over the parametrization ratio γ.
rows.value: MSE(γ) is increasing as a function of γ.
rows.note: The proposition also reports that the bias increases and the variance is unimodal, but this row records the test-risk measure relevant to V4.
rows.check: V4 removed. In this linear model p = d, so raising γ also raises the problem dimension with total signal fixed. It is not a capacity sweep on a fixed task. It bears on V6 only: optimally tuned ridge gives monotone MSE with no peak.

rows.measure: Total variance and ANOVA variance components
rows.baseline: The components Vs, Vi, and Vsl converge to finite limits on the threshold; no baseline for total variance is stated.
rows.value: Total variance diverges; Vsi and Vsli diverge, while Vs, Vi, and Vsl converge to finite limits.
rows.locator: Section 2.3.2, Theorem 7; proof in Appendix B.7
rows.note: The authors identify the sample–initialization interaction and the sample–label–initialization interaction as the diverging components in this limit.
rows.check: None. Variance diverges at δ = 1/π as λ → 0, through the Vsi and Vsli components. The diverging terms are interactions involving samples and initialization, not label noise alone.
